experiences/harris-prophet-west-africa/t: Prophet William Wadé Harris and the Ivorian mass movement
experiences/harris-prophet-west-africa/a: Paraphrase of Harris's statements recorded by visitors and of David Shank's reconstruction: while imprisoned in Liberia for political activity (1910), the Grebo teacher William Wadé Harris received a visit from the angel Gabriel, who called him to be a prophet, to burn fetishes and to baptise. From 1913 to 1915, dressed in a white robe with a cross-topped staff, a Bible and a calabash rattle, he walked along the coast of the French Ivory Coast and the Gold Coast, preaching against traditional 'fetishes', baptising perhaps 100,000-120,000 people, and directing converts to wait for teachers 'with the Bible'.
experiences/harris-prophet-west-africa/c: French colonial authorities expelled Harris in 1915, fearing unrest. When Methodist missionaries arrived in 1924 they found thousands of Harris converts awaiting them; others formed the independent Harrist Church.
experiences/harris-prophet-west-africa/a: Harris is honoured as a prophet of African Christianity who preached in an indigenous idiom, accepted polygamy among converts, and empowered African agency.
Mission churches in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana grew directly from his movement; Methodists honour his evangelistic role while distancing themselves from some practices.
Seen as a forerunner of African Pentecostalism's emphasis on power encounter, healing and deliverance from spirits.
Lamin Sanneh, Adrian Hastings and David Shank use Harris as a key case of African-led Christianisation outpacing Western missions.
experiences/harris-prophet-west-africa/d: Power encounter and the burning of traditional objects.
experiences/harris-prophet-west-africa/s:
William Wadé Harris was born around 1860 among the Grebo people near Cape Palmas in south-eastern Liberia, a country then dominated politically by the Americo-Liberian elite descended from freed African Americans. As a boy he lived with a Methodist minister and was converted; as a young man he worked as a seaman on ships along the West African coast. He later became a teacher and catechist in the Protestant Episcopal (Anglican) mission and served as a government interpreter. Like many Grebo, he resented Americo-Liberian rule, and in 1909 he was arrested for his part in a pro-British political movement among the Grebo, including the raising of a British flag.

In prison in 1910, according to what Harris later told visitors, the angel Gabriel appeared to him in a trance and called him to be a prophet of the last days. He was told to abandon his European clothes, to preach Christ, to destroy fetishes, the objects used in traditional religion, and to baptise. During his imprisonment his wife Rose died. After his release he dressed in a white gown and turban, carried a bamboo cross-topped staff, a Bible and a calabash rattle, and set out to preach, at first with little success in Liberia.

In mid-1913 Harris crossed into the French colony of the Ivory Coast, accompanied by women singers, and walked eastward along the coast and lagoons. His message was simple: give up fetishes and traditional spirit practices, worship the one God, keep Sunday, avoid alcohol and adultery, and be baptised. According to colonial and missionary reports, whole villages responded. People brought their traditional objects to be burned, and Harris baptised them by sprinkling water on their heads from a bowl, sometimes laying his Bible on them. Witnesses reported healings, and stories circulated of sudden misfortunes befalling those who mocked him.

He went on into the British Gold Coast (Ghana) as far as the Axim and Apollonia region in 1914, then returned to the Ivory Coast lagoons. Unlike most missionaries he did not require converts to give up polygamous marriages, which he himself practised, and he did not build a church organisation of his own. Instead he told converts to build chapels, appoint leaders, and wait for teachers who would come 'with the Bible'; some villages appointed twelve 'apostles' to lead them. Within about eighteen months he had baptised, by most estimates, between 100,000 and 120,000 people.

The French colonial authorities, at war in Europe from August 1914 and alarmed by a mass movement under an African prophet from British-influenced Liberia, arrested Harris and expelled him in early 1915. Many of the chapels his converts built were destroyed and some of his followers were persecuted. Harris returned to Liberia, where he continued to preach on a smaller scale until his death in 1929.

When British Methodist missionaries led by William J. Platt reached the Ivory Coast in 1924, they found tens of thousands of Harris's converts still meeting and waiting for teachers, and they absorbed many of them into the Methodist Church. Catholic missions also grew. In 1926 Platt sent Pierre Benoît to visit Harris in Liberia; Benoît brought back a statement which the Methodists presented as Harris's endorsement. Other converts, who rejected the missions' rules on polygamy and wanted an African-led church, formed the Harrist Church, organised by John Ahui, which is still active in Côte d'Ivoire.
experiences/harris-prophet-west-africa/k: William Wadé Harris is born, around this year, among the Grebo near Cape Palmas, Liberia.
He is arrested for his part in a pro-British political movement among the Grebo.
In prison he reports a visit from the angel Gabriel calling him to be a prophet.
Harris crosses into the Ivory Coast and begins preaching, burning fetishes and baptising.
He extends his mission into the Gold Coast, reaching the Axim and Apollonia region.
French authorities expel him after he has baptised perhaps 100,000-120,000 people.

Harris dies in Liberia; the independent Harrist Church develops in the following years.
experiences/harris-prophet-west-africa/s: Harris led what is often described as the largest mass movement to Christianity in West African history up to that time, achieved in under two years by an African prophet without missionary support. His career is a classic case of African agency in the spread of Christianity, a theme emphasised by scholars such as Lamin Sanneh and Andrew Walls. His ministry seeded Methodist and Catholic growth in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana and inspired African-initiated churches such as the Harrist Church and the Church of the Twelve Apostles in Ghana. It also raises lasting questions about power encounters with traditional religion, polygamy and church discipline, and the colonial suppression of African prophets.
experiences/kimbangu-healings-nkamba/tit: Simon Kimbangu's healing ministry at Nkamba
experiences/kimbangu-healings-nkamba/acc: Paraphrase of Kimbanguist tradition and colonial and Baptist mission records: in April 1921 the Baptist catechist Simon Kimbangu, who had resisted earlier calls he believed came from Christ, laid hands on a sick woman who was reported healed. For about five months crowds flocked to his village of Nkamba seeking healing; he preached against fetishes and polygamy and in favour of Bible reading. Belgian authorities, alarmed by the movement and by workers leaving their jobs, arrested him in September 1921; his death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment, and he died in prison in Élisabethville (Lubumbashi) in 1951.
experiences/kimbangu-healings-nkamba/con: Colonial officials saw a political threat; Baptist missionaries were divided. The movement survived underground and was legally recognised in 1959 as the Church of Jesus Christ on Earth by His Messenger Simon Kimbangu (EJCSK), which joined the World Council of Churches in 1969.
experiences/kimbangu-healings-nkamba/ass: Kimbangu is God's messenger and Nkamba is the 'New Jerusalem'; his suffering is seen as Christlike. Later Kimbanguist teaching attributed elevated spiritual status to Kimbangu and his descendants.
Many recognised a genuine evangelistic movement but have voiced concerns about later doctrinal developments regarding the Kimbangu family.
Seen as an early African healing revival, comparable to Harris and the Aladura.
Historians emphasise its anticolonial significance in Belgian Congo and its role as a model of African Christian independence.
experiences/kimbangu-healings-nkamba/deb: Later Christological teaching about Kimbangu and orthodoxy.
experiences/kimbangu-healings-nkamba/sto:
Simon Kimbangu was born in the late 1880s at Nkamba in the Lower Congo, among the BaKongo people, in what was then the Congo Free State and from 1908 the Belgian Congo. The region had endured the brutality of the Free State's rubber regime, and colonial rule weighed heavily through forced labour and taxation. Kimbangu was educated at the English Baptist Missionary Society station at Ngombe Lutete, baptised with his wife Marie Mwilu around 1915, and served as a catechist.

According to Kimbanguist tradition, during the influenza epidemic of 1918 he heard a call he believed came from Christ to care for the sick and preach. He resisted, feeling unworthy, and went to work in Léopoldville (Kinshasa), but the call continued. Tradition holds that on 6 April 1921 he laid hands on a sick woman in a neighbouring village and she was healed. The date is still celebrated by his followers.

News spread with remarkable speed. For about five months thousands of people came to Nkamba, which followers began to call the 'New Jerusalem', seeking healing. Kimbangu prayed for the sick, preached repentance, called people to abandon fetishes and traditional charms, condemned polygamy and dancing, and urged Bible reading and faith in God. Colonial and mission sources report that hospitals and mission stations emptied, and that workers left plantations and other employment to go to Nkamba. Other 'prophets' (bangunza) appeared in the region, some with more overtly anti-colonial messages.

Belgian officials and businesses grew alarmed, fearing a political uprising and economic disruption. Baptist missionaries were divided: some initially saw the movement as a genuine revival, while others worried about excess and their loss of control, and the Catholic missions were hostile. In June 1921 an attempt to arrest Kimbangu failed and he went into hiding. On 12 September 1921, according to his followers, he gave himself up voluntarily.

A military court at Thysville in October 1921 convicted him of endangering state security and sentenced him to death and 120 lashes. After appeals, including from Baptist missionaries, the Belgian King Albert commuted the sentence to life imprisonment. Kimbangu was transported to Élisabethville (Lubumbashi) in the far south of the colony, where he remained in prison for about thirty years until his death on 12 October 1951. Thousands of his followers were deported to remote parts of the colony, which unintentionally spread the movement.

The movement survived underground for decades despite repression. In 1959, shortly before Congolese independence, the Belgian authorities granted legal recognition to the Church of Jesus Christ on Earth by His Messenger the Prophet Simon Kimbangu (EJCSK), led by his youngest son Joseph Diangienda. The church grew into one of the largest African-initiated churches, with millions of members, built a great temple at Nkamba, and joined the World Council of Churches in 1969. In later decades some of its teachings about the divine status of Kimbangu and his descendants raised serious questions from other churches about its theological orthodoxy.
experiences/kimbangu-healings-nkamba/key: Simon Kimbangu and his wife Marie Mwilu are baptised at the Baptist mission at Ngombe Lutete.
During the influenza epidemic Kimbangu reports a call to heal and preach, which he at first resists.
According to tradition, he lays hands on a sick woman who is healed, beginning his public ministry.
Crowds flock to Nkamba for healing; colonial authorities grow alarmed.
Kimbangu surrenders to the authorities after months in hiding.
A military court sentences him to death; King Albert later commutes the sentence to life imprisonment.
Kimbangu dies in prison in Élisabethville after some thirty years' captivity.
The Kimbanguist Church (EJCSK) receives legal recognition under Joseph Diangienda.
The Kimbanguist Church joins the World Council of Churches.
experiences/kimbangu-healings-nkamba/sig: Kimbangu's brief ministry founded what became one of the largest African-initiated churches, and he is honoured in the Democratic Republic of Congo as a national figure who suffered under colonial rule. His story became a powerful symbol of African Christian independence and of the colonial suppression of African prophets, and historians use it to explore the interplay of religion, healing and resistance. The church's entry into the World Council of Churches was a landmark in the recognition of African-initiated churches by older denominations. At the same time, later Kimbanguist teaching on the divinity of Kimbangu and his sons has led many other Christians to question whether the church remains within historic Trinitarian orthodoxy.
